tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft's September Patch Tuesday update broke audio on some USB devices, and they haven't officially fixed it yet. After thirty years watching Microsoft patch days, I can tell you this is peak September energy: they release fixes for one thing and accidentally murder something unrelated, then we all become amateur audio engineers troubleshooting in Slack while someone's boss yells about connectivity.

tools-tech.dwp_take: Chase's CIO Gill Haus is saying his team focuses on AI fundamentals like strategy, governance, and talent development rather than just throwing engineers at coding problems. This matters because it's the difference between organizations that actually get value from AI versus those that end up with expensive chatbots nobody uses and technical debt for years. Here's the thing though: this isn't revolutionary advice, it's just competence. The real news is that a major financial institution is publicly admitting the basics matter more than the hype, which tells you how many other places are still doing it backwards.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft’s AI Code of Conduct aims to curb AI behavior

tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft published a draft code of conduct promising that AI models will remain under human control and subject to meaningful oversight. This matters to digital workplace pros because we're about to deploy these tools into production environments where they'll handle real work, real data, and real consequences, so knowing the vendors are thinking about guardrails is basic table stakes. The funny part is watching tech companies write pledges about controlling their creations right around the same time they're racing to make them more autonomous, so I'll believe "subordinate to humanity" when I see it actually enforced instead of just drafted.

tools-tech.title: Govern AI agents like workers. Just don’t pretend they’re human
tools-tech.excerpt: The newest member of the corporate workforce never sleeps, never asks for a raise, and can be cloned before lunch. It can also confidently make the wrong decision thousands of times before anyone noti
tools-tech.dwp_take: Someone's finally saying out loud what we've all been thinking: AI agents need actual governance frameworks, not just wishful thinking that treats them like junior employees who'll figure things out on the job. This matters because digital workplace leaders are already deploying these things into production environments where they can silently wreck customer data or approve fraudulent transactions while everyone's grabbing coffee. The irony is thick here: we spend years training humans with policies and oversight, but we'll deploy AI that can make a thousand bad decisions before anyone notices, then act surprised when it does.
